rules.rule_en: Combining a number of simple sentences into one new sentence is called as synthesis of sentences.
There are three types of synthesis of sentences: Combining of two or more simple sentences into a single Simple Sentence, a single Complex Sentence, or a single Compound Sentence.

A complex sentence is formed by joining two or more simple sentences with the help of subordinate conjunctions, while keeping the original meaning. It consists of a main clause and one or more subordinate clauses (Noun clause, Adjective clause, Adverb clause).
Noun Clause can be used as the subject of a verb.
Noun Clause can be used as the object of a transitive verb.
Noun Clause can be used as the object of a preposition.
Noun Clause can be used as the complement of a verb.
Noun Clause can be used in apposition to a noun.
Adjective Clause qualifies the noun or pronoun. Subordinate conjunctions used: Who, whose, whom, which, of which, that, as, why, when, where.

Adverb Clause modifies a verb, adverb or an adjective in some other clause using time clause conjunctions like: while, when, as, as soon as, before, after, by the time, until, till, whenever, small, as long as.
Condition Clause Conjunctions: if, unless, suppose, incase, on condition that, provided, i wish, i would, would that, if only.
Purpose conjunctions: so that, lest, in order that, that.
Place conjunctions: where, wherever.
Result: use 'such' or 'so' to combine sentences.
Reason: because, since, as, that, now that.
Concession or Contrast: although, though, as, even if, however, whether, even though, no matter what, not withstanding that, much as, whatever.

A compound sentence is formed by joining two or more simple sentences with the help of Co-ordinating conjunctions such as and, but, or, neither, nor, too, also, so, therefore, likewise, either...or, neither...nor, etc.
Combine two or more simple sentences into one compound sentence using coordinating conjunctions.
A Simple sentence is one which has only one Subject and one Predicate.
A Compound sentence is one made up of two or more Principal or Main Clauses.
A Complex sentence consists of one Main Clause and one or more Subordinate Clauses.
A Simple sentence consists of only one Finite Verb.
A Complex sentence has one Main Clause and one or more Subordinate Clauses.
A Compound sentence has two Main Clauses combined by a Coordinating Conjunction.
Compound sentences are formed by connecting two independent clauses using coordinating conjunctions like and, yet, or otherwise.
A simple sentence has only one finite verb.
A simple sentence consists of exactly one independent clause containing one subject and one predicate.
A simple sentence may contain subject complements, object complements, adverbial phrases, and non-finite verbs.
A phrase is a group of words without a finite verb that does not express a complete thought.
A clause is a group of words containing a finite verb; a subordinate clause depends on a main clause to complete its meaning.
Two Main clauses connected by a conjunction form a compound sentence.
Simple sentence: One finite verb, limited by person, number and tense; one subject and one predicate.

Compound sentence: More than one finite verb; two or more independent clauses connected by coordinate conjunctions (FANBOYS: for, and, not only but also, but, or, yet, still, so, otherwise, therefore).
Complex sentence contains one independent clause and one or more dependent clauses connected using subordinate conjunctions or relative pronouns.
Transformation patterns for Simple (Inspite + V+ing), Compound (But/Yet/Still), and Complex (Though/Although/even though).
Transformation patterns for Simple (In the event of/In case of/on+verb+ing), Compound (Or/not and/at once), and Complex (If/Unless/As soon as).
Transformation patterns for Simple (Being), Compound (And/and so/Therefore), and Complex (As/Since/Because).
Transformation patterns for Simple (As a result of/On account of/Because of/Due to/Owing to), Compound (And/and so/Therefore), and Complex (As/Since/Because).
Too...to (Simple) | Very...and so (Compound) | So...that...can/could not (Complex)
In order to (Simple) | And so (Compound) | So that (Complex)
Besides + V+ing (Simple) | Not only...But also (Compound) | As well as (Complex)
Without + V+ing (Simple) | Must...Otherwise (Compound) | After (Complex)
